problem:
Given a list of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two different elements whose sum equals target. Assume exactly one such pair exists; the indices may be returned in any order.

Example: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9 -> [0, 1]
Example: nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 -> [1, 2]

data.key_insight: As we iterate through the array, we can check if the complement (target - current_element) has already been seen and stored in a hash map.

steps.title: Initialize a hash map
steps.detail: Create an empty hash map to store numbers and their indices.

steps.title: Iterate through the array
steps.detail: For each element at index i, calculate its complement: target - nums[i].

steps.title: Check complement existence
steps.detail: If the complement exists in the hash map, we found our two numbers. Return the index of the complement and the current index i.

steps.title: Store current number
steps.detail: If the complement is not in the hash map, store the current number and its index in the hash map and continue.

data.pattern_summary: Use a hash map when you need to quickly check if a previously seen value exists in constant time, transforming O(n^2) searches into O(n).

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Storing elements in a hash map allows us to check for the required complement instantly.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers require the array to be sorted, which would destroy the original indices we need to return.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays of a certain size, not pairs that sum to a target across arbitrary positions.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Binary search requires sorted data and only helps find elements in O(log n) time, whereas a hash map gives O(1).

data.brute_force_idea: Check every possible pair of numbers in the list using nested loops to see if their sum equals the target.
data.brute_force_why: The outer loop runs n times, and the inner loop runs roughly n times for each outer iteration, resulting in n * n total checks.
data.bottleneck: The inner loop repeatedly scans through the array to find the second number, performing redundant work that we could avoid by remembering what we have already seen.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times you inspect elements after the current one.
Consider whether you really need a second loop to find a number you might have already passed.
Think about what data structure lets you check for the existence of a value in O(1) time instead of looping.

data.overview: The Two Sum algorithm finds the indices of two numbers in an array that add up to a target sum. It uses a hash map to store numbers and their indices as it iterates, allowing it to check for the required complement in constant time.
data.intuition: Imagine checking tickets at a coat check. As you receive each coat number, you calculate its matching pair to reach the target sum and check if you already filed that matching pair earlier. If not, you store the current coat and its claim check.

pitfalls: Using the same element twice by checking the hash map before inserting the current element when duplicate values could trigger a false match.
Forgetting that the problem guarantees a single solution, leading to unnecessary extra check code.
Using a two-pass approach that fails if duplicate numbers overwrite their indices improperly.

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly scans the remaining elements for every single number, causing an O(n^2) bottleneck. The optimized solution removes this by using a hash map to store numbers we have already seen. As we iterate through the array, we check in O(1) time if the needed complement already exists in the map.

derivation.note: The empty dictionary is initialized once.
The loop runs once for each element in the input list.
Arithmetic subtraction happens on each iteration.
Hash map key lookup takes constant time on average.
Executes at most once when the correct pair is found.
Stores the current number and its index in the hash map.

data.time_summary: Line 4 runs n times. Inside the loop, lines 5, 6, and 8 execute in constant O(1) time per iteration. Multiplying the loop count n by the constant work inside gives O(n) total time.
data.space_summary: The dictionary num_to_index stores up to n elements in the worst case, requiring O(n) extra memory.
data.takeaway: When you need to find historical elements that match a current value, trade search time for memory by storing previous items in a hash map.
mistakes: Forgetting to store the current element in the hash map after checking for the complement, which misses valid pairs.
Using a nested loop like the brute force solution, which scales quadratically instead of linearly.
Returning values instead of indices, violating the problem requirements.
